topic.angle: A self-referring sentence and how it echoes in Gödel's theorems

card.title: The sentence that disagrees with itself

panels.text: Read this sentence: 'This sentence is false.' Is it true, or false?
If it is true, then what it says holds, so it is false. If it is false, what it says is wrong, so it is true. Either answer leads to a contradiction.
This is the liar paradox, and it is old. The Epimenides paradox, around 600 BC, has been suggested as an early example.
In 1931 Kurt Gödel published his incompleteness theorems. He named the liar paradox as a loose analogue of his result.
His first theorem says that no consistent set of axioms that an algorithm can list is able to prove all truths about the arithmetic of natural numbers.

probes.question: Suppose 'This sentence is false' is true. What follows from what it says?
True or false: Gödel cited the liar paradox as an analogue of his incompleteness result.

claims.claim: Liar sentence: if true then false, if false then true
claims.note: Verified by calculation: true implies its content (false) holds; false implies its content is wrong so it is true; both cases contradict.

claims.claim: Assuming it true leads to contradiction, and likewise assuming the opposite
claims.quote: Similarly, we get a contradiction when we assume the opposite.

claims.claim: Epimenides paradox (around 600 BC) has been suggested as an early example
claims.quote: The Epimenides paradox (c. 600 BC) has been suggested as an example of the liar paradox
claims.note: Page adds that they are not logically equivalent; card says only 'suggested', which is fair.

claims.claim: In 1931 Goedel published his incompleteness theorems
claims.quote: These results, published by Kurt Gödel in 1931, are important both in mathematical logic

claims.claim: Goedel cited the liar paradox as an analogue of his result
claims.quote: Gödel specifically cites Richard's paradox and the liar paradox as semantical analogues to his syntactical incompleteness result
claims.note: Card's 'loose' analogue is the drafter's word; page says 'semantical analogues'.

claims.claim: First theorem: no consistent algorithmically listable set of axioms proves all truths about arithmetic of natural numbers
claims.quote: The first incompleteness theorem states that no consistent system of axioms whose theorems can be listed by an effective procedure
claims.note: Sentence continues: is capable of proving all truths about the arithmetic of natural numbers.
